topics.assessment: Ordinary-condition solid shape/volume description is appropriately qualitative. Many common solids, not every solid, are described as crystalline.

Long-range internal order includes atoms, ions or molecules. Regular exterior is a growth-dependent clue, not a sufficient universal crystal criterion. Salt cube and snowflake topics retained without claiming every salt grain has the same external shape.

Mica/graphite layer separation is correctly distinguished from breaking a layer internally. Layered carbon networks, pencil deposition and weaker interlayer binding preserve source topics. The original about-twofold layer-distance statement remains a source-attributed rough comparison, not a new precision measurement or universal bond-length identity.
Thermal/electrical and quartz optical direction dependence is stated property-by-property with many/may qualifiers. It does not claim every optical mode or every property varies with direction.

Anisotropy is defined for a specified physical property. The false universal inference that every property of every crystal must be direction-dependent is removed in modern prose only. Cubic-symmetry thermal/electrical conductivity can be isotropic; this is a valid specific example, not a claim that all cubic properties are isotropic.
Typical/common crystalline metal materials and their engineering uses retained. The prose explicitly avoids an exceptionless all-metals-crystalline rule.

Macroscopic near-isotropy is limited to some common polycrystalline metals and measured properties, not every material or processing state. The nearby following paragraph supplies the orientation condition.

Many grains, approximately random crystallographic orientation, absence of strong preferred texture and effective-property averaging are stated explicitly. Processing-induced texture may retain macroscopic directional dependence. Independent physical reasoning: an approximately rotation-invariant orientation distribution can suppress grain-level directional variation in a many-grain effective response; the text correctly uses approximate/can language rather than promising isotropy under every microstructure or test.
Polycrystal means many crystal grains; single crystal means one continuous crystal across the sample, not one constituent particle. No claim of defect-free perfection is added.

Controlled crystal growth and competing grains growing until impingement preserve the qualitative source topic. This is not an operation protocol or a numerical claim about identical nucleation times.
Sugar-block polycrystallinity is correctly conditioned on many small sugar crystals combined into the block; it is not asserted for every form of sugar.
